reason: A judges refactoring craft and risk management independent of tests while B specifically judges whether tests are used to drive the design/refactor, so a careful manual refactor without TDD scores high on A and low on B.

A judges whether failures are caught and surfaced with actionable context while B judges only the surface wording of failure strings, so a robustly handled error with a typo'd message scores high on A and low on B.

A bundles pyramid shape together with test-data realism and mocking discipline while B is limited to the ratio/speed of test types, so a suite with the right unit/integration/e2e mix but unrealistic fixtures or brittle mocks scores high on B and lower on A.
A judges the scope/size of the code change while B judges the formatting of the commit message text, so a large sprawling diff can still carry a perfectly formatted commit message and vice versa.

A is specifically about CAP-style consistency/availability trade-offs and conflict resolution while B is about general redundancy/backup/traffic-shaping resilience mechanisms, so a single-node service with solid backups and rate limiting scores high on B without any CAP trade-off reasoning at all.

A judges whether the code's architecture is decoupled and testable while B judges the rigor of the testing process/methodology itself, so well-decoupled code tested with an undisciplined ad hoc approach scores high on A and low on B.
Both criteria describe the identical fact that the PR includes tests covering the changed behavior, just in different wording.
Both criteria are the same paraphrased rule that tests should exercise externally observable behavior and avoid coupling to implementation internals.

A is a language-agnostic statement about module/class boundaries and visibility while B is specifically about idiomatic Rust crate mechanics (macros, extension traits, feature flags), so a crate with excellent macro/trait idioms could still have poor general module boundaries and vice versa.

A includes hygiene actions like removing unused/duplicate imports and resolving naming collisions while B is limited to placement/ordering/grouping formatting, so a file with zero unused imports but inconsistent group ordering scores high on A and low on B, or vice versa.

A is about the overall rigor and coverage of a codebase's testing methodology while B is specifically about tests being used as a design-shaping/TDD tool, so comprehensive but not test-first testing scores high on A and low on B.

A is about CI enforcement discipline such as never casually disabling checks and preferring autofix, while B is about the depth/actionability of the analysis findings themselves, so a strictly-enforced but shallow linter setup scores high on A and low on B.

A evaluates the resulting testable code structure while B evaluates the process of using tests to shape that design, so code architected testably without being built test-first scores high on A and low on B.
Both criteria describe the identical fact that the description states the motivation/reason for the change rather than just what changed.
Both criteria are the same rule paraphrased: prefer self-explanatory code and use minimal, accurate, why-focused comments.
Both criteria describe the same underlying quality that change/commit/PR messages should clearly and concisely explain what changed and why with adequate context.

A concerns named-vs-default exports, import consolidation, and type-only export syntax while B concerns ESM-vs-require syntax and relative/absolute path and export-placement conventions, so a file can follow one rule set well while violating the other.
